correctness.rationale: All statements quantify over prime powers q>=2 and n>=4, with legal third-vertex witnesses distinct from stationary anchors. Counting two-space neighbours by a projective intersection point gives degree d=q(q+1)[n-2]_q; adjacent and disjoint pairs have lambda=[n-1]_q-2+q² and mu=(q+1)² common neighbours. The six mutually exclusive adjacency-pattern witness counts are lambda,d-1-lambda,v-2d+lambda for adjacent anchors, and mu,d-mu,v-2-2d+mu for disjoint anchors. Their global minimum is six only at (4,2) and mu otherwise: q=2,n=4 has disjoint-pair common nonneighbours six, while for q>=3 or n>=5 all other counts exceed mu. Deleting fewer than that number preserves every pair pattern, and deleting one entire minimum witness set destroys its three-variable existential sentence. The standard three-pebble argument proves counting-free FO^3 equivalence to the Rado graph at arbitrary finite quantifier depth. The uniqueness of the minimizing pattern forces all minimal destructive sets to have the stated two classes. Independent parameter arithmetic checked 35 (n,q) cases, including nonprime prime-power values for integer formulas; no finite test is treated as the all-prime-power proof.

originality.rationale: Published Kneser, q-Kneser, and orthogonal-array FO^3 deletion results share the generic minimum-two-point-witness principle but use distinct vertex families and adjacencies. Full published orthogonal-array and ordinary Kneser proofs were compared: their explicit 6-count tables are not the Grassmann 2-subspace parameters and yield no automatic J_q(n,2) threshold. Pankov Grassmann embedding and Byrne–Byrne–Cioabă SRG VC studies are relevant but their inspected statements do not establish this universal deletion radius and minimum-set classification. Best-of-knowledge originality is restricted to the all-(n,q) Grassmann-specific phase change and exact minimum-destructive-set types; standard FO^3 pebble logic and general witness-minimum idea are prior art.

value.rationale: The all-parameter deletion threshold is a natural fault-tolerance invariant of classical Grassmann adjacency graphs, with a nontrivial exceptional four-dimensional binary case and a complete description of minimum destructive deletion sets. It answers which vertex deletions preserve an unrestricted-depth three-variable graph theory, not merely a restatement of graph degree or a finite experiment. The parameter calculations are elementary given strongly regular geometry but the uniform extremal deletion classification is mathematically useful as a canonical q-analogue example.

limitations: Pure adjacency and equality, ordinary counting-free FO^3; no higher-variable claim; all prime powers symbolic proof, numerical checks bounded.
Possible unlocated general SRG deletion theorem; no full review of all relevant external primary texts.
